webTitle: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says

fields.headline: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says
fields.trailText: US president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with family
fields.bodyText: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced. The US president revealed her departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving “so she can spend more time” with her family. The 28-year-old gave birth to a daughter, Viviana, in May, and returned from maternity leave last month. The departure of Trump’s most prominent spokesperson comes with his approval rating at a historic low as voters express discontent over rising prices and a war in Iran that has no end in sight. Trump said Leavitt, who became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary on his return to office in January 2025, “will now be one of my top outside advisors” in a post on his Truth Social platform. Leavitt wrote on X: “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary – and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.” Leavitt served Trump as a press aide during his first term in the White House. She ran for Congress in 2022 as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire’s first congressional district but lost the race. She joined Trump’s 2024 campaign and was transition spokeswoman before Trump selected her to ‌be White House press secretary. At 27 she was younger than Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he was Richard Nixon’s spokesperson. A devout Christian, Leavitt, wearing a cross necklace, and her team would hold a short group prayer before she walked into the briefing room to face reporters. The briefings rarely strayed off message or made headlines but did keep factcheckers occupied. For example, her claim that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people,” was rated false by Politifact. In a smooth delivery with few verbal stumbles, Leavitt zealously defended the president while berating Democrats and the “fake news” media. In her first appearance on the podium, she described Trump as “the hardest-working man in politics” with “wildly popular” policies responsible for a new “golden age”. Leavitt was cordial with reporters behind the scenes but could be combative in front of the camera. In January this year, when a journalist raised the killing of Renee Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, Leavitt demanded to know why Good had been killed. The reporter answered: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.” Leavitt, jabbing her finger, snapped: “You’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in the room as a journalist … You shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.” Trump often praised Leavitt as an effective communicator and drawing attention to her appearance. He once told the Newsmax network: “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.” On Wednesday the president’s allies joined the acclaim. Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, tweeted: “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.” Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, added: “Karoline Leavitt has been the most successful Press Secretary in history. Always strong, clear and right to the point … We are all Karoline Leavitt fans!” Democrats, however, took a different view. Adam Schiff, a senator for California, posted: “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.” Trump did not outline plans for who might succeed her. He had four press secretaries during his first term. Sean Spicer is now a political commentator and podcaster; Sarah Huckabee Sanders is now the governor of Arkansas; Stephanie Grisham is now a fierce critic of Trump who spoke at the 2024 Democratic national convention; Kayleigh McEnany is a host on Fox News.

webTitle: Mike Lindell refuses to concede in Minnesota primary despite getting far fewer votes

fields.headline: Mike Lindell refuses to concede in Minnesota primary despite getting far fewer votes
fields.trailText: With almost all votes counted in Republican primary for governor, Lisa Demuth is ahead by over 10% of ballots
fields.bodyText: Mike Lindell, the pillow salesman, Trump supporter and election denier, has refused to concede defeat in Minnesota’s Republican gubernatorial primary, despite trailing by a double-digit margin the morning after polls closed. The Associated Press called the race for Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, late on Tuesday night. With almost all votes counted, Demuth was more than 45,000 votes ahead of Lindell, who had the backing of Donald Trump, beating him by 43.4% to 32.5%. Businessman Kendall Qualls, backed by the Republican state party, was trailing in third. Told by a reporter on his own streaming channel, LindellTV, that the AP had declared the race over, Lindell dismissed the wire service outright. Asked why he wouldn’t accept the call, he questioned the AP’s authority to determine the outcome and insisted hundreds of thousands of votes remained uncounted. “I’m not going to give up this race until the votes are counted,” Lindell said. “That’s nonsense.” Lindell did not return a request for comment on what steps he will take next to contest the election, as he waits for the votes to come in. Lindell built his political career on the claim that Trump’s 2020 defeat was the product of a rigged and stolen election, spending what he has said were tens of millions of dollars pursuing that conspiracy theory through lawsuits, documentaries and conferences, even as courts repeatedly threw it out. Last month he settled a $1.3bn defamation suit brought by voting technology company Liberty Vote, formerly known as Dominion Voting Systems, regarding the stolen election lies. Lindell’s campaign was also dogged by questions over his own eligibility to run. He was, for weeks, not registered to vote in the state whose governorship he was seeking – his registration remained active in Texas, tied to a property owned by a company in Lufkin, even as he told reporters he had re-established Minnesota residency. Minnesota’s same-day registration rules meant he could still cast a ballot, and run, regardless. Trump, who has failed to carry Minnesota in three consecutive presidential elections, made a late, personal push for Lindell on Tuesday, urging Minnesota Republicans on social media to hand him a decisive win and praising his commitment to “free and fair” elections. Lindell’s defeat extended a run of losses for Trump-endorsed candidates, including House races for Andy Ogles, a representative in Tennessee, and Amir Hassan, a navy veteran in Michigan who lost to a candidate who had dropped out. Demuth, who becomes the first woman to win a Minnesota Republican gubernatorial nomination, called the result a milestone but said her campaign’s work was “not done yet”. She will face Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic senator who easily won her own primary, in November’s general election to succeed the retiring governor, Tim Walz.

webTitle: Trump ally loses, mixed results for progressives: takeaways from primaries in Minnesota, Wisconsin and beyond

fields.headline: Trump ally loses, mixed results for progressives: takeaways from primaries in Minnesota, Wisconsin and beyond
fields.trailText: Primaries across US included Darline Graham advancing to runoff, while progressive Francesca Hong and MyPillow’s Mike Lindell fell short
fields.bodyText: A series of primary elections on Tuesday shaped the future of both the Democratic and Republican parties, pitting newcomers against established candidates and testing name recognition. Wisconsin, Minnesota, Alabama, South Carolina, Vermont and Connecticut held elections, with a gubernatorial race in Wisconsin capturing nationwide attention. That election, in which progressive challenger Francesca Hong faced David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, was seen as another key test of the left wing of the Democratic party in a swing state. Democratic socialist falls short in Wisconsin Despite polls suggesting she was on course for victory, the progressive state lawmaker Francesca Hong was narrowly beaten in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor by David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive. The result amounts to a stunning upset after a messy campaign, during which Crowley exited the race, only to re-enter it – and promptly received the endorsement of Tony Evers, the outgoing Democratic governor. It comes after a wave of leftwing candidates won prominent Democratic primaries in recent months, including Abdul El-Sayed, running for US Senate in Michigan, last week. Hong had pointed to Crowley’s return in the campaign as evidence of panic by the Democratic establishment, although Crowley insisted he was “far from” the establishment. The fight for a new generation of Democrats prevails in Connecticut Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford, ousted the incumbent congressman John Larson in Connecticut’s first congressional district, the AP projects. Larson, 78, has represented the district since 1999. Bronin, 47, talked to the Guardian last year about Democrats challenging older members of Congress in the aftermath of Joe Biden’s 2024 exit from the presidential race over age and mental fitness concerns. At the time, Bronin said Democrats needed to be “relentless and clear” about the ways Donald Trump is making life worse for Americans, and “equally relentless and clear” about the Democratic party’s vision for improving their daily lives. In a statement on Tuesday, Bronin said: “Tonight, voters sent a message that if we are going to fix this mess we’re in, we need to build a Democratic Party that’s bringing a whole new energy to this fight. It’s time to be courageous, bold, and clear about who we’re fighting for and what we’re fighting for.” Alabama voters cast ballots again in redrawn district that dilutes Black voting power Some Alabama voters took to the polls for the second time this primary season after the state’s Republican-controlled legislature reconfigured four of the seven districts. The redrawn district map came after the US supreme court dismantled a key section of the 1965 Voting Rights Act and several southern states moved to redistrict and consolidate Republican power. In June, the supreme court ruled that Alabama could use a redrawn congressional map that eliminates one of the state’s two majority-Black districts in this year’s midterm elections. The new map poses steep challenges for Shomari Figures, the Democratic representative who was first elected in 2024 after the creation of a new district that included the mostly Black cities of Mobile and Montgomery. But the district no longer includes Mobile, Figures’s home town. Rhett Marques, a Republican state representative and small-business owner who became part of the new district, won the primary to challenge Figures in November. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, advances to runoff in South Carolina Republican primary Interim US senator Darline Graham advanced to a runoff in South Carolina’s special Republican primary to replace her brother, Lindsey Graham, in the Senate one month after his sudden death. She will face Congressman Ralph Norman, an ultraconservative Freedom Caucus member, on 25 August. The winner of that contest will run against Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, in the November general election. Trump-backed Graham was appointed to the Senate after Lindsey Graham died one month ago. A political outsider, she has sought to cast herself as focused on affordability, not national security like her brother. Trump ally Mike Lindell loses significantly in Minnesota governor primary Mike Lindell, the CEO of MyPillow and a staunch Trump ally lost decisively to Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota house of representatives. Minnesota has not elected a Republican governor in decades, but the primary was still a test of Trump’s strength among his party in the state. Lindell’s loss could be attributed to the weakness of his campaign, but also a sign of Trump’s waning support amid low approval ratings. The known election denier did not concede when the race was called for his opponent. Demuth became speaker last year in an evenly divided house, becoming the first Black person in the role. The impact of Trump’s immigration agenda weighed heavily over Minnesota Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won decisively on Tuesday after a campaign that attacked Angie Craig, a US representative, on her immigration record. At the center of the attack was Craig’s vote for the Laken Riley Act, which requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, and Craig has since expressed regret for voting for it. The role of immigration enforcement served as a major issue in the primary after the state experienced devastation, including the deaths of two residents and hundreds of deportations, when the Trump administration sent in thousands of immigration officers in early 2026 as part of Operation Metro Surge.

webTitle: In Ohio, Haitians’ American dream shatters as ICE prepares to deport them

fields.headline: In Ohio, Haitians’ American dream shatters as ICE prepares to deport them
fields.trailText: US immigration has ramped up operations against Haitians, whose temporary protected status was removed by Trump
fields.bodyText: When Monsanto Maler walked out of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Blue Ash, Ohio, at 9.15am on Sunday with an ankle monitor freshly attached to his left leg, he put his hand over his face, burst into tears and fell to the ground. He had come to the US in June 2023, fleeing gangs in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, where he had been hit over the right side of his head, leaving a large, visible scar. Grief-stricken and unable to hold himself up, he collapsed on the ground, his dozens of immigration documents, which a moment before had been carefully packed under his arm, strewn across the concrete. His face was full of confusion, his eyes bewildered. His American dream had ended in humiliation and despondency, with a metal box tied around his ankle. “I feel depressed, physically, mentally. I feel dizzy,” he said through an interpreter. Four hours earlier, 75 miles (120km) to the north in Springfield, Viles Dorsainvil, who heads the Haitian Support Center, and Pastor Carl Ruby loaded into a sedan on a humid, foggy morning at 5.30am. They were about to embark on the drive south to the Blue Ash facility to help Haitians such as Maler in any way they could. On the drive, the pair talked about their efforts to help a family from Ruby’s church in Springfield emigrate to Quebec City, one of the thousands of Haitians forced to leave the US due to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies. “I was helping them pack. The dad had all this patriotic stuff with him,” said Ruby, who knows at least two Haitians from his congregation who have been called to Blue Ash to be fitted with ankle monitors. “It makes me sad that what he’s going to remember from the United States is that he had to leave.” Dorsainvil talked about a Haitian man who worked at a local Amazon warehouse, had temporary protected status (TPS) until 2029 and had come to his center last Friday seeking help. “When he got that letter [requiring him the come to the Blue Ash facility], he was terrified, he got sick,” Dorsainvil said. Dorsainvil, himself a TPS holder, and Ruby chatted about what was happening in Haiti right now – that a burger there cost $16 and how the absence of opportunity was pushing people into gangs or to flee the country for their lives. On 5 August, the Washington DC district judge Ana Reyes, whose ruling had previously prevented the Trump administration from lifting TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians, was forced to remove her stay, following a decision from the supreme court backing the Trump administration’s efforts. It means that for about 350,000 Haitians in the US on TPS, it’s an end for their lives in the US. Over the last decade, more than 12,000 Haitians moved to the Rust belt town of Springfield, where they worked in labor-intensive jobs in manufacturing and food packaging, jobs that local companies struggled to fill. But in September 2024, then presidential candidate Donald Trump falsely claimed that immigrants in Springfield were eating pets, setting off a firestorm of unrest that fueled neo-Nazi marches, bomb threats and school closures in Springfield, and the national immigration debate centered on the town of 60,000 people. In recent weeks, dozens of Haitian nationals living in Springfield – some who had applied for asylum, others who had TPS – have begun receiving emails from the Department of Homeland Security ordering them to show up at the Blue Ash facility, often early on a Sunday morning. The letter, a photo of which was seen by the Guardian, contained no stated reason for the requirement or an indication that a monitoring device would be attached to their bodies. According to advocates and lawyers representing the Haitian nationals, those who received the ankle monitors will not be allowed to travel more than 75 miles from their home without the consent of an immigration judge. The Blue Ash Ice office is at least 71 miles from Springfield. By 7am outside the Ice facility, streams of protesters – nuns and priestesses, children, and men wearing USA hockey jerseys – had positioned themselves along the road in front of the building. Aside from one marked DHS police vehicle parked outside, the ICE building, a single-story, red-brick office, had no obvious marking to indicate its use as a federal government facility. “Life there is extremely difficult. Haiti is the poorest country in the western hemisphere; [it’s a country] exploited for all of its resources,” said Lorne Hlad, a pastor from Cincinnati attending the protest, who has worked in Haiti and visited six times. “[TPS] should be renewed. Gangs control Port-au-Prince; there’s no active government. Sending people back to a country that has no infrastructure to protect them is inhumane.” At 7.40am, the first Haitian national, a man dressed all in black, arrived for his appointment. By 8am three people, including Maler, had arrived. Thirty minutes later, a Haitian man and woman arrived and were given communion by Ruby, who had brought a vat of wine, bread and a large gold cross. “We want to give them the message that Jesus is with them,” said Ruby. “The Bible isn’t policy, but the Bible is very clear that God loves immigrants. It teaches that they are to have access to justice.” Dorsainvil and immigration lawyers said they were assisting Haitians to file a motion for amelioration that could remove or replace the ankle monitors with monitoring devices worn on the wrist. “The wrist monitors may be slightly less stigmatizing,” said Heather Campbell, an immigration lawyer representing several of the Haitian immigrants. “But anything that differentiates you from somebody else, especially if you are part of a community that people know this is happening to, it’s going to make you uncomfortable.” Questions sent by the Guardian to Ice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking, among other things, the stated objective of attaching ankle bracelets to Haitian nationals, were not directly responded to. Instead, Ice shared a statement that read: “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.” Organizers of Sunday’s protest estimate that about 700 people showed up to support the Haitian immigrants. “It’s reminiscent of the shackles used during slavery, something the Haitian people are very familiar with, after liberating themselves from slavery in the late 18th century,” said Samantha Searl of Ignite Peace, the non-profit leading the protest action outside the Ice facility. “The ankle monitors send a message to all immigrants that they will always continue to be subjected to the violence of our punitive immigration system.” Facing midterm elections in November, recent polls show American public opinion is souring on the Trump administration’s Ice enforcement activity. A YouGov poll released on 21 July found that just 30% of those surveyed believe Ice has been using necessary and justified force in its activities. Having gotten back to his feet and walking a short distance from the Ice facility, Maler, still visibly reeling from what happened to him, was driven away by a friend in a small sedan car, his hopes and dreams of a better life in America shattered. On the drive back to Springfield, Ruby and Dorsainvil stopped at a McDonald’s. Ruby ordered an iced tea, Dorsainvil some ice water. Dorsainvil was clearly exhausted – he said he stayed up late the previous night working on his university thesis. “It’s a study of the economic impact of Haitian immigrants on Springfield,” he said.

webTitle: Anger after Trump’s secret flight swap appears to offer up staff and media as decoys | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Anger after Trump’s secret flight swap appears to offer up staff and media as decoys
fields.trailText: Democrats demand congressional briefing after passenger-laden Air Force One sent on decoy flight despite security scare
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Democrats have called for a congressional briefing after a charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited into a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill the president last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck. More than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain from Turkey, without being told there was a threat to their lives. “It appears that the idea was we can reduce the danger to President Trump by offering up 100 or so people to be killed by the Iranians in his place,” said Steven Cash, the executive director of the non-profit Steady State who is a former CIA intelligence officer and senior adviser to the Department of Homeland Security’s intelligence branch. How did the plot to smuggle Trump off the plane unfold? In this video, the Guardian breaks down the footage from that day, showing how the president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jet in view of television cameras, and then was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies before flight. David Crowley defeats Francesca Hong to win Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor David Crowley, a Milwaukee county executive, pulled off a last-minute victory after re-entering the Wisconsin governor’s race and defeating Francesca Hong. Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, ran on a platform that included free childcare up to 400% of the federal poverty level, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on the construction of new datacenters, which differentiated her from her Democratic colleagues in the governor’s race. Where have progressives enjoyed electoral success this week? Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won her Democratic primary for US Senate in a race centered on immigration enforcement. Flanagan, who beat the congresswoman Angie Craig, recently told the Guardian: “So often I think Democrats are like: ‘What do we think we can win?’ Instead of: ‘What are the fights that we should be picking?’” What happened in South Carolina’s abbreviated special Republican primary? Darline Graham, appointed to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey, will face the congressman Ralph Norman in a runoff on 25 August. The winner will face the Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November’s midterms. Judge blocks Trump’s order aimed at using USPS to restrict mail-in voting A federal judge on Tuesday blocked ⁠the US Postal ⁠Service from implementing part of Donald Trump’s executive order that aims ⁠to tighten rules for mail-in voting before November’s midterm elections. The ruling expanded on an ‌earlier order that had prevented Trump’s administration from implementing it in 23 mostly Democratic-led states. Where else are Trump policies facing a new legal challenge? The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other advocacy groups have asked a federal judge to block Donald Trump from enforcing his latest attempt to restrict eligibility for birthright citizenship. The supreme court previously said Trump’s original executive order, which he issued the day he began ⁠his second term in the White House, violated the 14th amendment to the US constitution. ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks ICE plans to spend up to $20m to purchase thousands of gloves for officers and agents that can deliver painful electric shocks, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security. The devices, called Glove (generated low output voltage emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies of Lexington, Kentucky. According to the manufacturer: “The discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds and leaves no burns, marks or scars.” It has advertised the device as a “humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution for many situations facing our men and women in uniform.” The gloves have previously been used in settings such as jails in the US. In other news … Colombian rescue workers are racing to find survivors after the country’s deadliest earthquake this century killed at least 240 people and left at least 3,000 missing. Firefighters and residents of south Lebanon have accused the Israeli military of lighting wildfires in the region, as forested areas burned down in blazes sparked by Israeli bombing. Gianni Infantino’s opponents are working together to produce a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as a system of patronage that the governing body Fifa has adopted under his presidency. The Bumble dating app said it was dropping its women-first messaging rule ⁠that has ⁠been a defining feature since its launch in 2014. Stat of the day: Samuel Alito gained up to $2.9m from oil and gas assets since joining supreme court Critics argue the US high court justice should recuse himself from an upcoming climate accountability case involving fossil fuel firms after a review of financial disclosures showed Samuel Alito gained up to $2.9m from his oil and gas interests between 2005 and 2024. Well Actually: The 11 biggest wellness trends of 2026 so far Every year, the wellness industry churns out new products and practices. Sometimes, these trends are legitimate. Sometimes they’re utter nonsense. Often they’re somewhere in between. Madeleine Aggeler lists the wellness trends that have provoked controversy and interest in 2026. Don’t miss this: Drowned the day her visa came through – the tragedy of a Moroccan footballer trying to reach Ceuta Faten Ben Omar El Azizi was among at least 141 people who died during last month’s mass crossing to the Spanish territory in north Africa. In the cruellest of ironies, on the day she drowned her mother was told that the footballer had just been granted a visa to go to Spain. This is their story. Climate check: Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame? The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadly. The Guardian’s environment editor, Damian Carrington, explains the multiple factors behind it. Last Thing: High school football player in Arkansas practises with viper in helmet Rather him than me – a Maumelle high school student felt unusual movement inside his headgear after warmups last week and discovered a slithering 2ft venomous cottonmouth. The snake was captured and released in a wooded area far from the school. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. webTitle: Minnesota progressive wins Senate primary over anti-ICE sentiments, as Wisconsin governor’s race remains close – as it happened

fields.headline: Minnesota progressive wins Senate primary over anti-ICE sentiments, as Wisconsin governor’s race remains close – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: That’s all for us for tonight. The big Wisconsin race is still outstanding: Francesca Hong, a Democratic socialist state lawmaker, and Milwaukee county executive David Crowley, are neck-and-neck in the race for Democratic nominee for Wisconsin governor. Republican Tom Tiffany easily secured his party’s nomination. In Minnesota, lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan handily won the Democratic primary for US Senate, beating moderate US representative Angie Craig in a race animated by anti-ICE sentiment. She will face Michele Tafoya in the general. In the Republican bid for Minnesota governor, House speaker Lisa Demuth scored an upset, beating pillow salesman Mike Lindell, who had gotten Trump’s endorsement. She will face Amy Klobuchar in the general. In hotly contested congressional races: Luke Bronin beat incumbent John Larson in Connecticut’s first congressional district. Matt Little won a three-way race in Craig’s district, Minnesota’s third congressional district. Michael Alfonso, the 26-year-old son-in-law of transportation secretary Sean Duffy, won the Republican nomination in Tiffany’s district, Wisconsin’s seventh congressional district. Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic primary in her third try to unseat Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s toss-up third congressional district. Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives, secured the Republican nomination for governor, edging out pillow salesman Mike Lindell, who had received Trump’s endorsement in the race. Demuth became speaker last year in an evenly divided House, becoming the first Black person in the role. Peggy Flanagan, the progressive lieutenant governor of Minnesota, clinched the victory in the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, beating out moderate US representative Angie Craig. The AP called the race, with Flanagan leading with nearly 59% of the vote. The AP has called a few more races: Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, won in the Democratic primary for Minnesota’s eighth congressional district, a right-leaning area, over Luke Gulbranson, who has been on the reality TV show Summer House. Jake Johnson, a math teacher, won the Democratic nomination for US House in Minnesota’s first congressional district Maurice Mercer, the former city council president of Pelham, won the Democratic nomination in a special primary election for US House in Alabama’s sixth congressional district Amanda Janoo, an economist who was running for office for the first time, secured the Democratic nomination for governor of Vermont over Aly Richards, a former head of a lobbying group, to take on incumbent Republican Phil Scott in November. With a lot of ballots still left to tabulate, progressive Peggy Flanagan holds a strong lead over moderate Angie Craig in Minnesota’s Democratic primary for US senate. Flanagan, the lieutenant governor, centered her attacks on Craig, a US representative, around immigration, hitting Craig over her vote for the Laken Riley Act. The law requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, and Craig has since expressed regret for voting for it. On the Republican side, pillow salesman and election denier Mike Lindell trails Minnesota House speaker Lisa Demuth in the governor’s race, despite Trump’s endorsement for Lindell. Michael Alfonso, the 26-year-old son-in-law of transportation secretary Sean Duffy, won the Republican primary in Wisconsin’s seventh congressional district. Alfonso was endorsed by Trump and Duffy to succeed Tom Tiffany, who is running for governor. If elected, Alfonso would be the youngest member of Congress. He doesn’t have much of a history in politics, but he did work for a time on Dan Bongino’s podcast. Rebecca Cooke, a “blue dog” Democrat, won a primary challenge by Emily Berge in Wisconsin’s third congressional district, a major target for national Democrats. Cooke will face Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden in November for the third time. In the last two elections, she came close to beating him. In a rare instance, she’s a relative moderate endorsed by progressive Bernie Sanders. The western Wisconsin district is a toss-up, and Cooke announced her third bid for the seat early. She grew up on a dairy farm and worked as a waiter, after running local businesses and working on Democratic campaigns. “I don’t know what people’s political background is, but when I’m shaking their hand, I’ll say: ‘I’m Rebecca Cooke, I grew up on a dairy farm,’ and I tell them a little bit about my background,” she told the Guardian last year. “By the end of the conversation, they go: ‘So, what party are you from?’ And I would rather that question if they’re agreeing with me on similar values.” Matt Little rose to the top of a three-way race among current and former state lawmakers to win the Democratic nomination in Minnesota’s second congressional district, the seat currently held by Angie Craig, who is running for US Senate. Little, who patrolled for immigration officers during Operation Metro Surge, defeated state senator Matt Klein and state representative Kaela Berg. He had received the endorsement from the state Democratic party via the delegate process. The second congressional district is seen as a swing district, though it went for Kamala Harris in 2024. Cook Political Report rates it as a likely Democratic seat, though national Republicans are likely to make a play to flip it. Results in the Wisconsin governor’s race are very close, with David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, narrowly leading Democratic socialist Francesca Hong. Crowley, endorsed by outgoing governor Tony Evers, made a last-minute full-court press across the state, emphasizing that he believes he is more poised to win statewide and beat Republican Tom Tiffany in the general. Polls had shown Hong with a strong lead, but often showed a sizable amount of undecided voters. With many candidates running, some dropping out and then Crowley re-entering the race, the polls likely didn’t accurately capture the race. Crowley’s team wrote a memo saying as much in the days leading up to the primary, stating that the polls would likely be off as they were in Michigan, where they showed Abdul El-Sayed with a large lead over Haley Stevens for US Senate. El-Sayed won the race, albeit with a closer margin than polls predicted. Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford, ousted incumbent congressman John Larson in Connecticut’s first congressional district, the AP has projected. Bronin, 47, was the latest Democrat to challenge an ageing member of Congress. Larson, 78, has represented the district since 1999. Bronin talked to the Guardian last year for a piece on Democrats challenging older members of Congress in the aftermath of Joe Biden’s 2024 exit from the presidential race over age and mental fitness concerns. At the time, Bronin said Democrats needed to be “relentless and clear” about the ways Trump is making life worse for Americans, and “equally relentless and clear” about the Democratic party’s vision for improving their daily lives. He said he wanted to see “an intense focus on issues like housing and healthcare and childcare”. In a statement tonight, Bronin said: “Tonight, voters sent a message that if we are going to fix this mess we’re in, we need to build a Democratic party that’s bringing a whole new energy to this fight. It’s time to be courageous, bold and clear about who we’re fighting for and what we’re fighting for.” Voters in South Carolina, Vermont, Alabama , Connecticut, Minnesota and Wisconsin took to the polls today.
